title: Temperature and Specific Energy Characteristics of Transient Microplasmas in Tomoiu Internal Confinement Fusion (TICF) Reactors
content: Tomoiu Internal Confinement Fusion (TICF) a hybrid chemical-thermonuclear process generates continuous net-positive thermal energy through the continuous formation of transient microplasmas rather than sustained confinement of a bulk plasma, thereby avoiding the plasma-instability challenges associated with maintaining high-temperature, long-duration plasmas in conventional fusion approaches. TICF is a hybrid chemical–thermonuclear process based on the continuous formation and interaction of transient, high-temperature microplasmas within a confined hydrogen–air–water reaction environment. The TICF utilize internally self-generated acoustic, electromagnetic, and magnetic energies to heat, compress and confine transient microplasmas without requiring externally supplied electrical power. The present study focuses specifically on the temperature and specific energy associated with transient microplasmas in the TICF Gamma-2 reactor. The experimental data analyzed were obtained during testing conducted at the City College of New York (CUNY–CCNY) by Professor Marco J. Castaldi and his team. During these experiments, no detectable gamma radiation and no indications of neutron-induced activation or structural degradation of reactor components were reported after several hundred hours of operation. Electrical signatures associated with positively charged particles and transient microplasmas bursts were also observed. These observations are interpreted as consistent with aneutronic nuclear processes involving protium and nitrogen species.
